div.head: Abt 15
div.ab: The common freeman’s right of protection [is worth] 6 shillings.
A commoner’s mundbyrd shall be 6 shillings.
The [breach of a] ceorl’s protection: six shillings.
[For violation of] a freeman’s protection, 6 shillings.

note.seg: Dieselbe Schillingzahl, aber anderen Wertes, gilt für den Schutz (s. d. Gl 15f.) des Gemeinfreien in Wessex. — Die Schutzrechtbusse steigt mit dem Stande (s. d. Gl 17b. g) in anderem Verhältnis als das Wergeld

The same number of shillings, though of a different value, applies to the protection (see that word in Gl 15f.) of the common freeman in Wessex. — The compensation for breach of protection rises with rank (see that word in Gl 17b. g) in a different proportion from wergild
For mundbyrd, see cap. 8, note 1 above.

It is difficult to find a satisfactory modern equivalent for the word ceorl, which denotes ‘freeman’ as distinct from ‘noble.’ ‘Commoner’ is less open to objection in the Kentish laws than in those of Wessex; but on the whole it seems preferable to ‘peasant,’ in both cases, although the latter would perhaps give a truer impression in general of the class specified.

note.label: ceorl’s
note.seg: Though modern English “churl” is the direct descendant of this word, the sense has changed so much that to use it would be misleading. Its normal Old English meaning is a peasant proprietor.

note.label: shillings.
note.seg: Whitelock, English Historical Documents, 392 states that the sense of ceorl, which I translate as ‘freeman’ throughout, is ‘peasant proprietor.’
